meta.title: Behind the Screen
meta.theme: what a change in shortlists after screened auditions can and cannot show

format.format_verified: 2026-09: recent CAT papers set Para Summary among the non-negative verbal questions; re-verify against each new official paper

apex.claim: Because a screen removes only what a panel can see while leaving the sound unchanged, a change in shortlists shows that something visible was contributing to the verdict, but does not identify what that something was.
apex.scope: Screened auditions and the inference the change licenses; the claim establishes the existence of a visual contribution, not its nature.

meta.learning_objective: separate what an experiment establishes from the explanation a reader supplies for it

quality.adversarial_review: The live rival is the option that concedes the experiment cannot name the factor and calls it discrimination regardless. The concession disarms the obvious objection, so the item turns on the list the author gives: a candidate's bearing, a reputation attached to a face, and nothing more articulate than an expectation about what a player of an instrument looks like. Two of the three are not discrimination in any ordinary sense, and the paragraph says outright that the experiment does not say which. The option about identical sound reports the premise that licenses the inference rather than the inference; the option about all judgements made in the presence of the judged widens a single controlled comparison into a standing presumption about judgement everywhere.

blind_solve.notes: full agreement; key reworded 2026-09-13 to carry the recommendation the paragraph itself makes, so that a prescriptive option is no longer a reliable negative signal; awaits re-solve; a distractor rewritten 2026-09-13 to carry a genuine concessive clause, so that conceding no longer marks the key; awaits re-solve

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General reasoning about what a screened audition can establish; no specific study or orchestra adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: An item about the gap between an existence claim and an identification. Three distortion families: addition (the mechanism named), structure (the premise promoted), scope (the claim lifted out of auditions).

sentences.text: When orchestras began hearing candidates from behind a screen the composition of their shortlists changed, and the change is evidence about the panel rather than about the playing.
The sound reaching the judges was the same in both arrangements; only what they could see had been taken away.
So whatever the screen removed had been contributing to the verdict, and it was not part of the performance.

What it was, the experiment does not say: the panels may have been reacting to a candidate's bearing, to a reputation attached to a face, or to nothing more articulate than an expectation of what a player of that instrument looks like.
The screen shows that something visible was being counted; it does not say what.

ideal_summary: Since only the visible was removed while the sound stayed the same, the change in shortlists establishes that something a panel could see was being counted, without establishing what it was.

builder.prompt: In one sentence: what does the paragraph say the screen establishes, and what does it leave open?

checks.ask: Does your sentence say what the screen establishes about the panel, rather than what it did to the shortlists?
checks.kept: Good. The change in shortlists is the observation; the claim is what that change licenses, which is that a visible factor was being counted.
checks.drifted: Reporting that the lists changed leaves the inference unmade. The paragraph's work is the step from an unchanged sound to a conclusion about the judges.

checks.ask: Have you named what the visible factor was?
checks.kept: Exactly right. The author offers three candidates and declines to choose, so a summary that chooses has done something the experiment could not.
checks.drifted: Bias is the name most readers supply. The paragraph lists bearing, reputation and plain expectation among the possibilities, and says the experiment does not decide.

checks.ask: Is your sentence about auditions, or about judgement in general?
checks.kept: Well held. The argument runs on one feature of this arrangement, that the sound was identical and only sight was removed.
checks.drifted: A claim about every judgement made in someone's presence covers interviews, examinations and trials, none of which supplies the controlled comparison this argument depends on.

question.stem: Which option best captures the essence of the paragraph?

options.A: Though the experiment cannot name what it was, the change in shortlists after screens shows that panels had been discriminating on grounds unrelated to the music.
options.B: Since only the visible was removed, the change in shortlists should be taken to show that something a panel could see counted, without showing what it was.
options.C: The sound that reached the judges was identical in both arrangements, and the only thing taken away from them was the sight of the person who was playing.
options.D: Any judgement made in the presence of the person being judged should be assumed to be affected by things that have nothing at all to do with the performance.

explanation.paragraph_meaning: Put a screen between the panel and the player and the lists of who gets through change. The music did not change: the same sound reached the same ears. The only difference was that the judges could no longer see. So something they had been seeing was going into the verdict, and it was not part of the playing. What that something was is another matter. It might have been how a candidate carried themselves, or a face the panel recognised, or nothing sharper than a vague sense of what a player of that instrument looks like. The screen proves that a visible something counted. It does not tell you its name.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option makes the inference the paragraph makes, from an unchanged sound to a visible factor in the verdict, and stops where the paragraph stops, at an existence claim without an identification. The closing sentence states that gap as a rule about what the screen does and does not show, which is why the summary may state it the same way.

distractors.why_wrong: The concession is the paragraph's own and it is not the objection that matters. The three possibilities the author lists include a reputation attached to a face and nothing more articulate than an expectation of what a player of that instrument looks like, neither of which is discrimination as the word is normally used, so naming the factor that way decides what the paragraph refuses to decide.
distractors.seductive_element: It admits that the mechanism is unnamed and then names its character anyway, which reads like a careful writer drawing the only conclusion still available; it is also the explanation almost every reader supplies for this result.
distractors.thinking_mistake: Conceding that a cause is unidentified while quietly classifying it, and mistaking the classification for what the experiment showed.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the premise that makes the inference possible, reported on its own. The conclusion drawn from it, that something visible was contributing to the verdict, is what the paragraph exists to state.
distractors.seductive_element: It is precisely accurate and cannot be faulted against the text, which makes it feel like the safe choice.
distractors.thinking_mistake: Summarising the controlled comparison rather than what the comparison was set up to show.

distractors.why_wrong: The argument depends on a feature peculiar to this arrangement, an identical sound with only sight removed. Interviews and examinations offer no such comparison, the paragraph never mentions them, and 'should be assumed' turns a single controlled result into a standing presumption.
distractors.seductive_element: It states the general moral the audition seems to illustrate, and general morals read like the deeper reading; a rule for other cases sounds like the useful thing to take away.
distractors.thinking_mistake: Turning a claim licensed by one controlled comparison into a presumption about judgement everywhere.

explanation.reading_habit: Distinguish 'something was doing this' from 'this was doing it'. An experiment that removes one variable proves the first; the second is a name you supplied.

mentor.challenge: The paragraph proves that something was counted and then refuses to say what. One option says it anyway.
mentor.takeaway: Knowing that a factor mattered is not knowing which factor it was.
